title: the DSG underground environment

banner.title: THE DSG UNDERGROUND ENVIRONMENT OPENER, R530: printed pp. 65-68 (pdf 66-69) - the first DM-section child, the underground environment chapter: the why-an-ecosystem justifications (defense: the dungeon safer than a castle - impervious to aerial attack, the earthquake target hard to identify at depth, held by a smaller group since access is limited, no wall garrison so a reserve against break-ins, the burrowers menacing but rarely marshalled; the drow and duergar survival through defensibility; mining: the dwarven and gnomish economies, the mines converted to fortresses, prisons and lairs, the burrowing monsters passageways, the connected limestone caverns many over 100 miles long; gravity: the centuries of creatures falling into holes and adapting to the dark world), the features of the underground game (the DM control over narrow options, the essential encounter in a central room, the plannable monster tactics with the rigged alarms and ambushes undoable by creative play, the beginners decision ease with the doorway and 10-foot-corridor defense, the danger atmosphere, the common fears, the alienness and wonder, the frontier below the feet with its exploration, scouting, plunder and conquest missions, and the back-to-basics variety), the nature of the underground environment and its denizens (the precarious balance of power upset by PC arrival, the land more precious than on the surface, the evil tendency with the drow and kuo-toa war banishment, the lower-planes theory and the oldest mind flayers and derro, the humorless philosophy with the functional art and the punished waste, the timelessness and the old-age-before-execution tale, the stubborn conservatism, the depth-shaped resources with the mile-floated wood and the raided food and slaves, the depth-shaped alienness, the sunless food chain with its fungi, rothe and cave pigs, the inedible stone-eaters, the minor scavengers, the nocturnal raiders, and the natural oxygen circulation through arctic shafts and geothermal heat), and a brief history of underground cultures (the five ancient cultures - the jermalaine tunnels, the myconid coexistence, the aboleth Darksea cities, the evicting cloakers, the mind flayer dominion checked only by low reproduction; the Alignment Wars with alignment-chosen sides and the seaborne kuo-toa; the evil halted at the sunlit tunnel mouths; the defeat, the retreat of drow and duergar and kuo-toa and the faded alliance; the immigrant niches; the interplanar doors with the Plane of Earth strongest; the gem-lusting svirfneblin, the stone-working pech and the interbred derro; and the savage wars of today with the isolated pockets between monster stretches)
banner.provenance: the DSG scan (archive.org item advanced-dungeons-dragons-1st-edition), pdf = printed + 1; the text read from the IA djvu OCR (djvu.txt lines ~8226-8860) with the pdf Acrobat-Capture layer as the second read (idx 149-162 = the printed pp. 65-69 windows); the compiled-tables appendix has no reprint of this prose. A CLEAN-READ ROUND: both machine reads agree on every load-bearing number - the 100-mile limestone caverns, the 10-foot corridor, the mile-or-more floated wood, and the five ancient cultures; the only garbles are the standing glyph classes (the Cyrillic-lead djvu noise on the DM table of contents, a page this round does not pin). SEAMS: the Monster Manual burrowers (umber hulk, landshark, xorn), the Monster Manual underground cultures (jermalaine, myconid, aboleth, cloaker, mind flayer, pech, derro, svirfneblin), the DMG inner planes (the Plane of Earth gate), and the R503 re-grain (this child of the DM section). THE DM SECTION OPENS with this round; the gap children for the underground geography (p. 69), the theories of the underground (pp. 70-71) and the cultures of the underdark (pp. 73-74) follow in later rounds. Nothing auto-credits.

consts.name: dnugLimestoneMiles
consts.comment: thousands of huge natural limestone caverns, many of them over 100 miles long, are now connected by the tunnels of miners and burrowing monsters.

consts.name: dnugCorridorFt
consts.comment: outnumbered PCs hold a better defensive position in a doorway or a 10-foot-wide corridor than they could in a wilderness clearing.

consts.name: dnugWoodFloatMiles
consts.comment: wood, the most common surface resource carried underground, can be floated a mile or more below via streams and rivers of sufficient depth - though few waterways flow hard enough to carry it without jamming.

consts.name: dnugAncientCultures
consts.comment: five distinct cultures are identified as dating back to ancient times in the underground: the jermalaine, the myconids, the aboleth, the cloakers and the mind flayers.

bools.name: dnugDungeonSaferThanCastle
bools.comment: a dungeon is a more secure position than a castle: virtually impervious to aerial attacks, hard to target with earthquake spells when it lies well beneath the ground, and held by a much smaller group of defenders because access is limited.

bools.name: dnugBurrowersNoArmy
bools.comment: burrowing creatures such as umber hulks, landsharks and xorn still menace dungeons, but are rarely marshalled into an army - and such a force would threaten a castle as much as a dungeon.

bools.name: dnugDepthBlocksExcavation
bools.comment: a dungeon can be built at any depth; the farther from the surface, the more effort an attacking army must spend excavating an access, unlike a castle with only a few dozen feet of stone.

bools.name: dnugNoGarrisonReserve
bools.comment: dungeon-dwellers need not garrison a wall, so they are much more likely to hold a reserve of troops against a sudden break-in.

bools.name: dnugDefensibilitySavedDrow
bools.comment: this defensibility probably accounts for the survival of the drow and duergar: after near-total defeat on the surface they slunk into the Underdark, withstood the final assaults and prospered - almost unassailable below, but little threat above, an uneasy balance.

bools.name: dnugMiningExcavation
bools.comment: the mining economies of dwarves and gnomes account for great excavation, and many old mines became fortresses, prisons or monster lairs; burrowing monsters like purple worms, umber hulks and ankhegs create passageways smaller creatures can use.

bools.name: dnugGravityPopulates
bools.comment: gravity populates the depths: creatures fell into surface holes for centuries, and where food and essentials existed they prospered, forgot the sunlit ways and adapted to the dark world.

bools.name: dnugDmControlNarrow
bools.comment: in the underground game the DM exerts great control over options and challenges: a room with two corridors gives the characters only three real options, so the DM prepares for only a few courses of PC action.

bools.name: dnugEssentialEncounter
bools.comment: an essential encounter can be forced by placing it in a centrally located room PCs are almost certain to visit regardless of the routes they choose.

bools.name: dnugMonsterTacticsPlanned
bools.comment: monster and NPC tactics can be planned in advance because approach directions are limited - alarms rigged and ambushes set with confidence - though intelligent and creative play can undo many a DM-rigged surprise.

bools.name: dnugBeginnersDecisionEase
bools.comment: the narrowness of options also eases the players decision-making, appreciated by beginners in particular, and confining terrain simplifies combat tactics.

bools.name: dnugDangerAtmosphere
bools.comment: the darkness, tight passageways and distance from succor create an atmosphere of intensity and excitement virtually unheard-of in a wooded or city setting.

bools.name: dnugCommonFears
bools.comment: the underground touches fears common to us all - caves and old mines where only experts dare tread, the real-life dangers of volcanoes and earthquakes, and the mythological sources of evil below - letting players role play the forbidden reaches at no risk save an imaginary character.

bools.name: dnugAliennessWonder
bools.comment: the players unfamiliarity with the underground adds to the sense of wonder; the DM needs a great deal of information to run it as a believable and interesting locale even while it stays mysterious to the players.

bools.name: dnugFrontierBelowFeet
bools.comment: both meanings of frontier apply underground - where civilization ends and where one government or culture yields to another - and the frontier below the feet of a civilized area is often more accessible, and perhaps more challenging, than the farthest national boundaries.

bools.name: dnugFrontierMissions
bools.comment: expanding the subterranean frontier means missions of exploration, scouting, plunder and conquest; the knowledge carried back is valuable to the ruler, and the desire to expand a frontier is often motivation enough for an expedition.

bools.name: dnugBackToBasics
bools.comment: underground adventure need not be a routine of slaying and looting: Underdark civilizations as old or older than any surface culture offer encounters as sophisticated as the court of the High King, and bored players can be drawn back by a mature story line - variety in settings, stories and conflicts being crucial to interest.

bools.name: dnugPrecariousBalance
bools.comment: whenever PCs intrude into the crowded underground realms, the DM should find the cultures in a precarious balance of power - unstable, so the arrival of surface characters may be enough to upset the equilibrium.

bools.name: dnugLandMorePrecious
bools.comment: underground races stake and defend territorial claims fiercely; land is even more precious below because solid rock often prevents a displaced race from moving freely elsewhere.

bools.name: dnugEvilTendency
bools.comment: the deep-dwellers show a tendency toward evil: the drow and kuo-toa were driven underground losing an ancient war against the united surface forces, evil banished to the less appealing locations - though evil remains on the surface too, and alignments drifted over time.

bools.name: dnugLowerPlaneTheory
bools.comment: another theory links the deep cultures to the lower planes, but the evil Underdark worship may follow a previously existing alignment rather than the depth itself - most meritorious for the oldest races with no surface period, the mind flayers and derro.

bools.name: dnugNoHumor
bools.comment: underground cultures have little appreciation for humor: the tons of rock overhead and the chances of asphyxiation or flood make life very serious, their art almost universally portrays death as omnipresent, and laughter is almost unheard of in the deep reaches.

bools.name: dnugDisciplinedIndividuals
bools.comment: many underground races are chaotic in nature, but that alignment shows mainly in large-group organization; individuals, lawful or chaotic, are very disciplined, the scarcity of resources - most notably air - forcing care.

bools.name: dnugFunctionalArt
bools.comment: underground art serves a function beyond merit: sculpture worked into support columns and arches, songs carrying solemn vows and formal introductions, and encyclopedias ranked among the highest forms of literature.

bools.name: dnugWastePunished
bools.comment: waste of food, material or energy is deplored and often punished severely; air is a valuable resource, and control of its use - particularly regarding fires - is a common feature of underground law.

bools.name: dnugTimelessness
bools.comment: with no day into night or summer into winter, a timelessness marks underground philosophy - the aging of creatures and plants the truest indicator, and even that meaning little; the tale is told of a captured surface man sentenced to immediate execution who died of old age in his cell first.

bools.name: dnugStubbornConservative
bools.comment: creatures raised underground are very stubborn and resistant to change; the most conservative surface government would seem radical by comparison - solid rock around them seriously limits the options when decisions are required.

bools.name: dnugDepthShapesResources
bools.comment: surface resources are common only in the top several hundred feet of the Underdark, except where gravity moves them deeper; wood is the most common, floated down waterways or harvested from rare solid-stemmed woody fungi.

bools.name: dnugFoodSlavesRaided
bools.comment: food and slaves are additional resources harvested by the denizens - slaves and food on the hoof moving under their own power; most underground creatures grow no crops and keep no herds, preferring raids on surface food stores.

bools.name: dnugDepthShapesAlienness
bools.comment: the farther below the surface, the less human the cultures: the drow, duergar and svirfneblin homelans lie very deep, while the much more alien mind flayers and aboleths dwell deeper still.

bools.name: dnugSunlessFoodChain
bools.comment: the underground food chain begins with fungi, lichens and molds that grow without sunlight; herbivores like rothe and cave pigs subsist on them, and intelligent creatures domesticate the herbivores to insure fresh meat, while unintelligent creatures eat what they can catch.

bools.name: dnugStoneEatersInedible
bools.comment: unusual life forms subsist on stone, gems or minerals; quite alien, they generally stand outside the food chain and are believed inedible to carnivorous or omnivorous hunters.

bools.name: dnugScavengersMinor
bools.comment: the scavengers living off carrion, garbage and offal occupy a very minor place in the food chain, since few carnivores find them palatable.

bools.name: dnugNocturnalRaiders
bools.comment: creatures living close enough to emerge and return in a single night prefer supplementing their supplies with nocturnal raids for surface plants and animals.

bools.name: dnugOxygenCirculation
bools.comment: oxygen must be circulated even to the deepest reaches: cold air sinks into huge arctic shafts, geothermal heat warms it and sends it rising through the domain until it emerges at entrances - a natural process needing no forced movement, though stagnant pockets occur unless circulation is improved.

bools.name: dnugJermalaineTunnels
bools.comment: the jermalaine spread through virtually all the underground realms and created most of the small narrow tunnels that first connected widely separated caverns - too small for most creatures to pass, later expanded and organized by other dwellers.

bools.name: dnugMyconidCoexistence
bools.comment: the myconids, basically peaceful but capable of defending themselves against the jermalaine, learned to coexist with little friction - their differing food sources meant no fight for the same ecological niche.

bools.name: dnugAbolethDarksea
bools.comment: the aboleth, evil creatures of extremely high Intelligence and advanced culture, prefer the dark subterranean waterways; their population concentrates in sprawling cities on the floor of the Darksea, developed with little interference - but ineffective outside water, unable to extend their influence.

bools.name: dnugCloakersEvict
bools.comment: the cloakers have dwelt underground since time immemorial, so alien few other creatures can communicate with them; they move into areas excavated by others and drive the original inhabitants away with deadly persistence.

bools.name: dnugIllithidDominion
bools.comment: the mind flayers once controlled vast reaches and were feared throughout the lands of darkness, none of the original races able to stand up to them; only their very low reproductive rate prevented control of the entire Underdark, and race wars have since driven them into deep hidden realms.

bools.name: dnugAlignmentWarsSides
bools.comment: the Alignment Wars were a single grand conflict spanning centuries with occasional truces of a few decades, characterized by great interracial cooperation and intraracial combat - the sides determined by alignment, not race, with the kuo-toa choosing evil in the seas.

bools.name: dnugEvilHaltedAtSun
bools.comment: the evil creatures bore an intense dislike for the sun, so their expansion halted at the mouths of their tunnels and caves - rarely would one venture onto the surface even in the dark of a moonless night, and rarely would a surface-dweller dare the world below.

bools.name: dnugDefeatAndRetreat
bools.comment: the forces of good slowly drove evil back until the survivors acknowledged defeat and bitterly sought shelter underground: the drow and duergar moved below in great numbers, their war skills overcoming the prior tenants; the kuo-toa entered the subterranean waterways; the tired victors abandoned the pursuit and the grand alliance faded.

bools.name: dnugImmigrantNiches
bools.comment: the newly arriving races carved out niches: the mind flayer and cloaker domains were severely reduced as drow and duergar seized caverns and tunnels, the kuo-toa claimed many small dispersed areas, the jermalaine and myconids stayed prosperous though somewhat crowded, and only the serene aboleths were left undisturbed.

bools.name: dnugPlaneOfEarthStrongest
bools.comment: the excavation of many cubic miles of rock, coupled with powerful spell-casters, opened gateways to other planes: the Plane of Earth connection the strongest, its denizens callable at will, doors to the lower planes developing, and doors to the Planes of Fire and Water where volcanic rock bubbled or waterways flowed - an unusually high population of a plane denizens often betraying a nearby gate.

bools.name: dnugSvirfneblinGood
bools.comment: the deep gnomes, or svirfneblin, adapted completely underground through lust for gems and are one of the few cultures with tendencies toward good; the pech arrived from perhaps the Plane of Earth with unsurpassed stone-working skill; and the derro, most recent, grew from duergar interbreeding with vaguely human races.

bools.name: dnugSavageWarsToday
bools.comment: savage warfare has erupted in the crowded realms since the retreat and continues with the same savagery today - once-overpopulated areas now desolate, populations whittled to isolated pockets of drow, duergar, myconids, derro, pech, cloakers, mind flayers and jermalaine between uninhabited or monster-inhabited stretches, while the aboleth keep age-old control of the still waters of the Darksea.
